To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the PrP sequences of the eight cetacean families are similar to those of other mammals, that they are close to the PrP sequences from species where natural TSEs have been described, that they are very similar to the PrP gene of the Delphinidae family, and that the phylogenetic tree obtained from the PrP sequences is in accordance with the species tree.
the PrP genes of the cetaceans analysed are very close to species in which natural forms of prion diseases are known, and therefore the occurrence of TSEs in cetaceans cannot be excluded.
the PrP sequence in the cetacean species analysed here is typical for eutherian PrP sequences.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of PrP sequences in cetaceans.
the PrP gene in cetaceans, which are the largest group of mammals and are the only mammals that are completely marine.
the comparative analysis of the PrP protein and the PrP gene in different species of cetaceans, with the aim of determining whether these animals are susceptible to prion diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cetacean PrPs have the potential to develop prion diseases.
the PrP genes of cetacean species show a typical eutherian PrP gene sequence.
cetacean species are potentially susceptible to prion disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the PrP sequence is highly conserved among cetaceans, but that the PrP amino acid sequence of cetaceans has some differences from that of other mammalian species.
cetacean species have a PrP gene that has the typical features of euterian PrP gene and that is close to species where prion diseases occur.
the PrP genes of cetaceans show a high level of variability, which could reflect the high level of variability found in cetaceans.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the cetacean genome contains a PrP gene, which, like the human and bovine gene, is susceptible to prions.
the PrP sequence of the family Delphiniade is identical, and the PrP sequence from Balaenoptidae and Ziphididae is different.
the cetacean species are not a homogeneous group and that the PrP genes of different species are not identical.
